title: Using domain walls to benchmark fast quantum anneals
authors: Shushmi Chowdhury, Asa Hopkins, Nick Chancellor, Viv Kendon
abstract: We consider the distribution of domain walls arising in ground states of frustrated 1-dimensional Ising spin chains with anti-parallel boundary spins. For ideal chains, a sine-squared particle-in-a-box distribution of domain walls is expected in the quantum setting, and a uniform distribution expected classically. However, for chains with random imperfections, prior work [Chancellor et al., npj Quantum Inf. 8, 73, 2022] found that the distribution in a physical implementation corresponded to neither. Instead, the domain wall distribution forms a U-shaped profile arising from a classical model with random fields, where the combination of averaging over these fields and thermal averaging produces the characteristic U-shape. With D-Wave's newer fast anneal feature, we access anneal times shorter than the coherence time and observe the expected coherent quantum behavior in the form of a sine-squared distribution. For the shortest available anneal time, the dynamics have not yet reached the sine-squared shape and instead display a different U-shape in the middle of the chains. This motivates using the extent of the domain wall distribution tail in this regime as a platform independent metric that provides a signature of both coherence time and noise levels.
summary: This work uses the behavior of domain walls in frustrated Ising spin chains to benchmark the performance of fast quantum annealers. By comparing the observed distribution profiles to theoretical predictions for quantum, classical, and disordered regimes, the authors propose using the domain wall tail length as a robust, hardware-independent metric for quantifying coherence and noise in quantum computation.
main_problem: The paper benchmarks fast quantum annealers by analyzing the distribution of domain walls in frustrated 1D Ising spin chains.
main_result: The tail length of the domain wall distribution in the fast anneal regime is proposed as a platform-independent metric to characterize both coherence time and noise levels.
method: The authors compare theoretical predictions (sine-squared vs. U-shaped) with experimental measurements on a D-Wave quantum annealer, analyzing how the annealing speed affects the observed distribution.
model_or_system: The system is a frustrated 1D Ising spin chain with anti-parallel boundary spins, modeled by a time-dependent Hamiltonian. The analysis focuses on the distribution of domain walls arising in the ground state.
key_observables: Domain wall distribution profile, tail length of the distribution, total and single domain wall occurrence counts.
important_parameters: Annealing time (fast vs. standard), coupling strength (J), disorder strength ($\zeta$), and temperature/thermalization regime ($ eta$).
main_assumptions: The metric relies on the domain wall behaving as an effective quantum particle in the coherent regime, and the analysis distinguishes between thermalized and coherent dynamics.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate schematic domain wall distributions for ideal quantum/classical cases and those with random fields. Later figures show probability distributions of domain walls for various anneal times and hardware settings.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the theoretical expectation for domain wall distributions (ideal vs. random fields) to applying this concept to the D-Wave hardware, comparing results across different annealing speeds and analyzing systematic hardware effects like gauge dependence.
why_interesting: The study provides a concrete, measurable diagnostic tool (domain wall tail length) derived from fundamental many-body physics to assess the performance and coherence of near-term quantum hardware.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Schematic showing an Ising chain of L = N + 1 spins with twisted boundary conditions imposed by longitu- dinal fields ±h on spins 0 and N + 1, with a single domain wall between spin sites N −1 and N. The N possible domain wall positions are labeled above and the N + 1 spins are la- beled below. Ferromagnetic coupling strengths J are applied between neighboring spins.

FIG. 2. Illustration of the expected domain wall distribu- tions for classical (top row) and quantum (bottom row) ideal (left) and with random fields (right) frustrated spin chains in their ground states (single domain wall).

FIG. 3. Outline of the experimental settings on the D- Wave quantum annealer. Problem instances are submitted using both the standard anneal protocol with an anneal time of 20 µs, and the fast anneal protocol with times of 0.005 µs, 0.01 µs, 0.03 µs, and 20 µs. In the fast anneal protocol, a flux bias is applied since non-zero local fields (hi) cannot be directly specified. A chain length of L = 10 was used in the standard protocol with 562 chains embedded across the available hardware qubits, and L = 12 in the fast anneal protocol with 468 chains embedded. Due to maximum QPU run time constraint per submission, the 10 000 were divided into four batches.

FIG. 4. Probability distribution from the fast anneal proto- col averaged over 468 chains for a chain length of 12 with 104 runs for different anneal times. The data have been post selected to only show single domain wall instances. On average across 468 chains per run the single domain wall count is 7072.9 ± 11.2 for 0.005 µs, 9119.4 ± 17.4 for 0.01 µs, 9960.9 ± 26.7 for 0.03 µs, and 9762.9 ± 21.3 for 20 µs (see table II). Error bars represent the uncertainty obtained by combining in quadrature the propagated binomial uncertainty from finite domain wall occurrences and the standard error of the mean across chains.

Figure 4 shows the domain wall distributions for anneal times of 0.005 µs, 0.01 µs, 0.03 µs and 20 µs. We observe a fair approximation of the sine-squared particle-in-a-box profile at 0.01 µs. This behavior was anticipated in [17], but short enough anneal times were not available then. The profiles at longer times of 0.03 µs and 20 µs show the emergence of the U-shape after thermalization that was reported in [17]. The fastest anneal runs, 0.005 µs yield a slightly skewed M-shaped profile, U-shaped in the middle with turned down ends.
